text: {"answer": "For most healthy adults, daily vitamin D supplements are not universally required, but they can be a reasonable choice for certain groups. Major bodies such as the US Institute of Medicine (now the National Academies) set a recommended dietary allowance of about 600 IU (15 micrograms) per day for adults up to age 70, and about 800 IU for those older. Many people obtain adequate vitamin D from sunlight, fortified foods, and a varied diet, but sun exposure varies widely with latitude, season, skin pigmentation, and sunscreen use. Adults who are older, housebound, have darker skin, live far from the equator, have limited dairy or fortified food intake, or have malabsorption conditions such as Crohn's disease or celiac disease may benefit from supplementation, and clinicians often recommend it for them. Routine high-dose supplementation is not recommended for everyone, since excess intake can cause hypercalcemia and kidney problems. A practical approach is to ask a doctor whether a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D is warranted, and to avoid megadoses unless prescribed.", "confidence": 72}
